Inquisition. A formal Church tribunal established to identify and punish heresy, most notably the Roman or Holy Office Inquisition founded in fifteen-forty-two by the Catholic Counter-Reformation. It became infamous in the context of the scientific revolution for investigating scientists whose ideas, particularly heliocentrism, contradicted Church doctrine, culminating in the trial of Galileo Galilei in sixteen-thirty-three. While often exaggerated in popular accounts, the Inquisition's institutional scrutiny of scientific claims exemplified the tension between empirical inquiry and religious orthodoxy during the Renaissance and early modern period.

The Roman Inquisition was established in fifteen-forty-two as a permanent papal institution to investigate doctrinal violations across Catholic lands. Galileo Galilei was tried by the Inquisition in sixteen-thirty-three for advocating heliocentrism, a model the Church condemned as contrary to Scripture. He was placed under house arrest for the remainder of his life.

Copernicus' heliocentric theory was placed on the Church's Index of Forbidden Books in sixteen-sixteen. His book remained readable by scholars with papal permission. The Inquisition prosecuted for heresy broadly, including challenges to Trinitarian theology and papal authority. Its involvement in suppressing science was limited compared to direct theological cases.

Torture was technically permitted under Inquisitorial procedure but was subject to restrictions and canonical appeals, making actual use variable and less systematic than common portrayals suggest. The Inquisition's power derived from its authority to impose spiritual censure, excommunication, and secular penalties like imprisonment and execution, enforced through cooperation with civil authorities.

Fear of Inquisitorial investigation may have self-censored some scientists. Many continued publishing and corresponding freely, suggesting institutional power was more effective against heretical theology than against natural philosophy. The tension between the Inquisition and scientific thought symbolized the broader conflict between dogmatic authority and empirical evidence that propelled the scientific revolution.

Galileo Galilei was tried and convicted by the Inquisition for defending heliocentrism. Heliocentrism was the theory the Inquisition explicitly opposed and condemned. The scientific revolution was the intellectual movement that eventually superseded Inquisitorial authority over natural philosophy. Copernicus' heliocentric theory was censured but remained influential despite Inquisitorial prohibition. The Renaissance was the intellectual and cultural period during which the Inquisition emerged as an institutional force.
